newsitem.title: USA: NYS lawmakers narrow differences over budget.
newsitem.headline: NYS lawmakers narrow differences over budget.

text.p: New York State's lawmakers Thursday agreed that they had narrowed some of their differences over the state's budget, now at risk of being four months late, but noted they still face some several hurdles.

Governor George Pataki told reporters in Albany, after meeting with the top two legislative leaders, "We are closer than we were, which is progress, but there are still very real differences, and I appreciate that they are difficult for all of us."
While New York State has been slammed for its chronically late budgets, which have been cited as one reason for its low credit rating, the state is getting one big benefit.
By relying on a series of interim, short-term spending measures that essentially hold spending level with the previous, 1997 fiscal year, the state is saving money.

This savings could propel a big, expected rise in revenues even higher. That gain has been estimated at around $2.2 billion, though estimates are sketchy as budget negotiators have agreed not to release details. Still, one of the main engines of the state's economy, Wall Street brokerage houses' profits, helped New York City end its fiscal year on June 30 with about a $2 billion cash surplus.

State Senate Majority Leader Bruno gave a slightly lower estimate of what the final 1998 fiscal budget likely will total, estimating it at in the neighborhood of $67 billion, around $1 billion less than published reports. He offered one of the more optimistic assessments of the talks, which were expected to resume later in the day, saying "I think we are in the range of being able to do a budget in the short-term."
The state budget talks still were stymied by unrelated issues.

For example, a fight over reapportioning the 12th Congressional District in Kings and Queens Counties in Manhattan has become part of the talks. Pataki said he was discussing the issue with Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, and Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan. The lawmakers face a July 30 deadline or risk having a court appoint an official to redraw the district.

Silver, the top Democrat lawmaker, said his plans for a $2 billion school bond act--which would have to be approved by August 4 in order to be put on the November ballot--was his main emphasis. "I think educating children is probably the greatest priority that we have in this budget."

When asked about the proposed school bond, Pataki said only "We are looking at it." And his fellow Republican, Bruno, said that whether a school bond act was included depended on whether the state did a full budget, or relied on more interim measures.

Among the issues that remained unresolved were whether the state should pick up the tab for providing Food Stamps for legal immigrants, as Washington stops paying for their benefits on August 22. Other matters included reductions in sales and gross receipts taxes, new prisons, and other welfare issues.

While the state's bond board, the Public Authorities Control Board, last week handed Pataki a victory when it approved a plan for the Long Island Power Authority to partly take over the Long Island Lighting Co. by selling $7.3 billion of debt, the full plan has yet to be finalized. Asked whether the LIPA plan would be in the budget, Silver replied "It may, but the details are, you know, we really haven't worked it out."
